blocks.text: A punched-card deck made a survey calculation portable between a data-preparation room and a computer. Each card held a fixed set of characters or numbers. A run of cards could encode observation values, point identifiers and instructions, so long as the fields and order were agreed in advance.

blocks.text: For a survey office, repeatability was the gain: prepare observations once, run a calculation, correct the programme or inputs, and run it again. Card punching and checking took time, and a missing or mis-sorted card could send staff back to the source book to find where the sequence broke.

blocks.text: The computer might return a coordinate list, but a list of positions is not automatically a map database. Unless the data also identified which points formed a boundary, which line continued across a sheet edge, or which record described each feature, the machine had no usable feature model to preserve. Chapter 3 follows the point where New Zealand systems began capturing and editing that linework itself.
